newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Radio talk show conjures spirits, beers and wines.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Radio talk show conjures spirits, beers and wines.

text.p: It's an obsession, a passion, a calling, their sustenance. For Gary Regan and Paul Pacult, alcohol is a way of life.

But don't expect to see this jovial pair at a drying-out clinic any time soon. Far from being their downfall, Scotch malt whiskeys, British stouts and California merlots have propelled Regan and Pacult to the top of their field -- as alcohol writers.
Between them, they have tasted thousands of alcoholic beverages and written six books and hundreds of articles for Playboy, Food & Wine and other publications.
"From eight to twelve each morning, I do tastings," Pacult said, describing a typical workday. "I taste about 40 wines, beers and spirits a week -- never more than 80."
"That's a lot," marvelled Regan, who specialises in spirits and cocktails. "I only do about 15 a week."

Now, Regan and Pacult are bringing their encyclopaedic knowledge of all things fermented to the airwaves with a radio programme devoted to alcoholic beverages. "The Happy Hour" began airing in January and is broadcast live on New York's WEVD every Saturday afternoon.
The shows are rambling, quirky and informative. Regan and Pacult rattle off their picks of the best drinks, snippets of alcohol industry news and historical anecdotes.

There is always a main subject such as craft-brewed beers, Italian wines or American whisky. Regan and Pacult interview experts such as Scottish distiller Evan Cattanach or Rosemary Zraly, author of "Champagne Uncorked."

And they urge listeners to "get into the spirit" and call them with questions. One caller asked if grappa could be chilled; another said he had three bottles of single malt scotch and needed to know the order in which to try them.
SPIRIT OF THE TIMES

In many ways, "The Happy Hour" capitalises brilliantly on the current cultural obsession with cigars and bourbon, manliness and sophistication. Regan and Pacult have no problem attracting advertisers like Makers Mark whiskey and Laphroaig scotch, who pay more than $300 for a 30-second spot. Seagram America and United Distillers U.S.A. also have signed on as sponsors.

The response from spirit producers, who often come under fire for advertising, was so overwhelming, in fact, that the show has been able to expand to two hours a week. Regan and Pacult also say they are in syndication negotiations and expect to go national by mid-year.
"The time is right," Pacult said. "The interest in alcohol is like an escalator going up right now with no end in sight."

The pair attributes the growing appreciation for fine drinks to globalization and the increasing availability of imported spirits, wines and beers. That, in turn, has created a domestic "Renaissance," especially in micro-brews or craft-brewed beers.

"Once people try these drinks, they're not going to say, 'To hell with this, let's drink something with no flavor and cheap,'" said Regan, who also credits groups like Mothers Against Drunk Drivers for spawning a quality over quantity mentality.
Despite the shift from Bud to Beaujolais, however, Pacult says Americans still lag behind Europeans in their alcohol culture. Their mission is to help their listeners play catch-up.
PUB SON MEETS WINE LOVER

What keeps "The Happy Hour" from being a self-indulgent and droning ode to the fine points of alcohol is Regan and Pacult's light-hearted banter. The two often disagree and playfully chide one another for bad taste. In one show Regan professes his love for Encantado, a Mexican spirit that makes Pacult's stomach turn. Pacult does not do cocktails, Regan knows nothing about wine.
In real life, the two, who have been friends for seven years, appear as different as their tastes in drink. The paths that led them to their career as alcohol gurus are also vastly different.
Regan, a ruddy British expatriate, sports a Santa Claus beard and an infectious belly laugh. Born in the pub that his parents owned in Lancashire, he began tending bar at age 14.
"That really formed a lot of my thinking," he said. "The pub is the community centre, that's where life revolves around."

Regan's life continued to revolve around alcohol when he moved to New York in 1973 and worked as a bartender and restaurant manager. In 1990 he won writing assignments on single malt scotches and British pubs in New York and was hooked.

Regan, author of the authoritative "Bartender's Bible," often collaborates with his wife Mardee Haidin Regan, a food writer. They live in Cornwall-on-Hudson in a house equipped with a 200-bottle Art Deco bar. Their next book, "New Classic Cocktails," is due out this spring.

Pacult's introduction to alcohol came much later in life, when he was contracted to do a landscaping job at a vineyard while attending college in Berkeley, California. He ended up working at the winery for 10 years and also began writing articles on wine that were snatched up by editors.

"The strength of my writing is that I really understand production, not just for wine but for beer and spirits as well. When I pan something I really know what I'm talking about," said Pacult, whose book "Kindred Spirits" will be published this year.

During the taping of "The Happy Hour," Pacult often reaches for an elegant silver flask of Scotch, and after wrapping up a show the two usually head across the street from WEVD's Seventh Avenue studio to the neighbourhood bar.
Last Saturday, Pacult sat nursing a Coke. "I'm driving," he said apologetically.
